name: chronic pain overview
title: Chronic pain: pain over 3 months is mostly a processing problem, so everyone gets education and supervised exercise first; then the drug is matched to what the pain looks like (tissue source, neuropathic, poor sleep, low mood), adjuvants come before opioids, and a patient who is not responding is referred and gets an opioid trial only under the START principle; below, acute vs subacute vs chronic pain, what each team member does, and which opioid to step to and how to switch

root.title: Pain over 3 months: which treatment matches THIS patient?
lines: mostly a PROCESSING problem (sensitized nervous system) · goal = manage pain and function, NOT cure
acute phase first: fully investigate and treat the injury, then early return to low-impact activity

groups.title: Pick the drug by what the pain looks like
lines: adjuvants before opioids · multimodal · start low, go slow · short trials

pres.title: FIRST, for EVERYONE
lines: • EDUCATE: hurt does NOT equal harm; the injury has healed, so activity desensitizes
• EXERCISE, individualized and SUPERVISED: strength + flexibility + cardio (yoga, tai chi for back pain); good evidence
• passive modalities (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), ultrasound, laser, heat): very little evidence
• massage only WITH exercise and education
• psychology: see the PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS chart

head: h
Ongoing tissue source
the minority: chronic nociceptive
tx: alone, or combined with tramadol or another opioid
watch: longer: monitor kidney function + blood pressure

head: h
Neuropathic or centralized
the majority
watch: 1-2 weeks to work after each change

head: h
Pain + poor sleep
watch: for pain and sleep (mood needs 100-150 mg)

head: h
Pain + depression or anxiety
feat: Pain AND low mood or anxiety
tx: SSRI: no significant effect on pain alone

head: h
Refer to a pain clinic
multidisciplinary chronic pain clinic
tx: • high risk (Opioid Risk Tool): male, age 16-45, personal or family substance use, psychiatric history
• urine drug screen · taper benzodiazepines · signed agreement
• start low, go slow · no driving until the dose is stable
• aim 30% less pain or better function
• which opioid: see the panel below
watch: • history of addiction: strong recommendation AGAINST (under 20 mg morphine equivalent if used)
• active psychiatric disorder: weak against, stabilize first
• elderly: lower, slower, longer interval, stop benzodiazepines
• pregnancy: taper to the lowest dose or off
• taper 10%; slow by half once a third is left

panels.title: Acute vs subacute vs chronic
items: acute: SECONDS, at the same time as the cause · proportional to it · nociceptive
subacute: HOURS TO DAYS · primary or secondary hyperalgesia, allodynia, spontaneous pain · mostly nociceptive, some neuropathic
chronic: over 3 months · can outlast tissue healing · a long-term disease, big emotional part · mostly NEUROPATHIC, some nociceptive

panels.title: The team: who does what
items: physiotherapist: prescribes + supervises activity · MOBILITY, strengthening, flexibility · spinal mobilization, some acupuncture · modalities only as an add-on
occupational therapist: activity participation, PACING, modification, ergonomics for daily activities and work · optimize the activity, not avoid it
kinesiologist: GENERAL EXERCISE prescription and supervision
psychologist: group + individual therapy for DEPRESSION, ANXIETY · cognitive behavioural therapy, pacing · family education
physicians: review, trial drugs, interventions · long-term plan for the family physician · nurses: support, documentation, triage

panels.title: Opioids: which one, and switching
items: mild to moderate pain: codeine or tramadol → morphine, oxycodone or hydromorphone
severe pain: morphine, oxycodone or hydromorphone → fentanyl → methadone
switching from a HIGH dose: 50% or less of the morphine equivalent (+ breakthrough doses) · from a moderate or low dose: 60-70%
why: an EQUAL dose of a new opioid can be life-threatening after tolerance to a high dose
